Der Film exhibition poster

Josef Müller-Brockmann’s all-type poster for a film exhibition: the title slides across the sheet like a moving credit.

Rights

Context

Poster for the exhibition Der Film at the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich, 1960. Offset, 127 × 90 cm, printed by Graphische Anstalt J. E. Wolfensberger AG, Zürich. Object M-0314, Plakatsammlung. eMuseum, Museum für Gestaltung Zürich.

MoMA holds a copy: offset lithograph, 90.1 × 127.6 cm, gift of the Kunstgewerbemuseum Zürich, object 57.1960. MoMA. The Library of Congress holds another (POS - Switz .M65, no. 5). LoC.

Fonts In Use, citing the museum’s eGuide, reports that the title was set in Akzidenz-Grotesk, exposed on photographic paper at several positions and degrees of sharpness, and retouched with opaque white to suggest a horizontally moving film title. Fonts In Use.

The eMuseum holds many preparatory photograms, drafts, and a construction drawing for the poster, for example object 167053, donated by Shizuko Yoshikawa from the Müller-Brockmann archive.

Observed

  • A near-black field fills the sheet. The title sits low, in the lower third, and runs off the left edge.
  • “der” is in warm gray and “Film” is in off-white; the F of Film overlaps the r of der, so the two words interlock.
  • All small text is red, in two blocks: the museum and “Ausstellung” at top, dates and opening hours at bottom.
  • Both red blocks start on the same vertical line, aligned with the left edge of the F.
  • The typeface is a grotesque in lowercase for the title and upper- and lowercase for the text; nothing is centered.
  • The upper two thirds of the sheet is empty except for the two red lines.

Why it belongs

The poster shows how the style gets motion without illustration: overlap and cropping of one word do the work of an image.

The single left axis shared by the red text and the capital F is a visible grid decision in a layout that otherwise looks free.

Borrow

Hang all secondary text from one vertical axis and let the display word break it.

Use an empty field as the main surface. One very large word plus a few small lines can be a complete composition.

Overlap two weights or tints of the same word to suggest sequence or motion.
